'''Larry E. Overman''' is a Distinguished Professor of Chemistry at the [[University of California, Irvine]].  He was born in Chicago in 1943.  Overman obtained a B.A. degree from [[Earlham College]] in 1965, and he completed his Ph.D. in chemistry from the [[University of Wisconsin–Madison]] in 1969, under Howard Whitlock Jr.   Professor Overman is a member of the [[United States National Academy of Sciences]] and the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]].  He was the recipient of the [[Arthur C. Cope Award]] in 2003, and he was awarded the Tetrahedron Prize for Creativity in Organic Chemistry for 2008.

Overman's research is focused on the development of new chemical reactions, particularly  [[transition metal]] [[catalysis|catalyzed]] reactions,  and the application of those reactions toward the [[organic synthesis|synthesis]] of [[natural product]]s.  Overman is most known for the [[Overman rearrangement]], a [[Claisen rearrangement]] of [[allyl]]ic [[Alcohol (chemistry)|alcohol]]s to give allylic [[trichloroacetamide]]s.

==Career==
Overman's Ph.D. focused on the mechanism of rearrangements related to the biosynthesis of [[lanosterol]] from [[squalene oxide]] via [[lanosterol synthase]].  Overman has explained that this work gave him a lifelong love of [[rearrangement reaction]]s.<ref name="OvermanTetrahedronPrize">{{cite journal|last=Overman|first=Larry E.|title=Molecular Rearrangements in the Construction of Complex Molecules|journal=Tetrahedron|publisher=Elsevier|doi=10.1016/j.tet.2009.05.067|pmc=2902795|pmid=20640042|year=2009|volume=65|issue=33|pages=6432–6446}}</ref>  This was followed by two years as a postdoctoral fellow at [[Columbia University]] with [[Ronald Breslow]], using non-covalent binding of [[cyclodextrin]] as a model of enzyme binding.

Larry Overman began his career at University of California, Irvine in June 1971.  The Irvine graduate program was small and thus in his early work Overman frequently performed experiments himself,<ref name="OvermanTetrahedronPrize" /> including his initial discovery of the Overman rearrangement.<ref name="Overman1974">{{cite journal 
 | last = Overman 
 | first = L. E. 
 | title = Thermal and mercuric ion catalyzed [3,3]-sigmatropic rearrangement of allylic trichloroacetimidates. 1,3 Transposition of alcohol and amine functions
 | journal = [[Journal of the American Chemical Society]] 
 | year = 1974
 | volume = 96
 | issue = 2 
 | pages = 597–599
 | doi = 10.1021/ja00809a054| bibcode = 1974JAChS..96..597O 
 }}</ref>
Palladium emerged as the metal of choice for this reaction, and this led to a long-term interest in palladium catalysis, including the palladium(II)-catalyzed [[Cope rearrangement]],<ref name="OvermanKnoll1980">{{cite journal|last=Overman|first=Larry E. |author2=Frederick M. Knoll |year=1980|title=Catalyzed sigmatropic rearrangements. 5. Palladium(II) chloride catalyzed Cope rearrangements of acyclic 1,5-dienes|journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society|publisher=ACS|volume=102|issue=2 |pages=865–867|doi=10.1021/ja00522a082|bibcode=1980JAChS.102..865O }}</ref> and later work on intramolecular cascading [[Heck reaction]]s.<ref name="AbelmanOverman1988">{{cite journal|last=Abelman|first=M. M. |author2=Larry E. Overman |year=1988|journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society|publisher=ACS|volume=110|pages=2328–2329|doi=10.1021/ja00215a068|title=Palladium-catalyzed polyene cyclizations of dienyl aryl iodides|issue=7 |bibcode=1988JAChS.110.2328A }}</ref>

Overman has performed many total syntheses of natural products, beginning with (±)-[[pumiliotoxin|pumiliotoxin C]] (with Peter Jessup) in the late seventies.<ref name="OvermanJessup1978">{{cite journal|last=Overman|first=Larry E. |author2=Peter J. Jessup |year=1978|journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society|publisher=ACS|volume=100|pages=5179–5185|doi=10.1021/ja00484a046|title=Synthetic applications of N-acylamino-1,3-dienes. An efficient stereospecific total synthesis of dl-pumiliotoxin C, and a general entry to cis-decahydroquinoline alkaloids|issue=16 |bibcode=1978JAChS.100.5179O }}</ref>  This interest was spurred on by a 1977 sabbatical visit by [[Samuel J. Danishefsky]].<ref name="OvermanTetrahedronPrize" />

Overman has also worked extensively on the aza-Cope-Mannich reaction, originally designed<ref name="OvermanTetrahedronPrize" /> to solve a stereoelectronic problem in the total synthesis of [[gephyrotoxin]].<ref name="KakimotoOverman1979">{{cite journal|last=Kakimoto|first=Masa-aki|author2=Larry E. Overman |year=1979|journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society|publisher=ACS|volume=101|pages=1310–1312|doi=10.1021/ja00499a058|title=Carbon-carbon bond formation via directed 2-azonia-[3,3]-sigmatropic rearrangements. A new pyrrolidine synthesis|issue=5 |bibcode=1979JAChS.101.1310O }}</ref>

:[[Image:AzaCopeMannich.png|400px|left|an Aza-Cope Mannich cascade reaction]] {{clear-left}}

This reaction is described by Overman as "robust",<ref name="OvermanTetrahedronPrize" /> and was subsequently used in the total syntheses of several natural products, for example (–)-[[strychnine]].<ref name="KnightOverman1993">{{cite journal|last=Knight|first=Steven D.|author2=Larry E. Overman |author3=Garry Pairaudeau |year=1993|journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society|publisher=ACS|volume=115|pages=9293–9294|doi=10.1021/ja00073a057|title=Synthesis applications of cationic aza-Cope rearrangements. 26. Enantioselective total synthesis of (−)-strychnine|issue=20 |bibcode=1993JAChS.115.9293K }}</ref>  A ring-enlarging version of the reaction was used in the synthesis of secondary metabolites such as actinophyllic acid.<ref name="MartinOverman2008">{{cite journal|last=Martin|first=Connor L.|author2=Larry E. Overman |author3=Jason M. Rohde |year=2008|journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society|publisher=ACS|volume=130|pages=7568–7569|doi=10.1021/ja803158y|pmid=18491907|title=Total synthesis of (+/-)-actinophyllic acid.|issue=24|pmc=2654095}}</ref>  A related reaction, a [[Prins reaction|Prins]]-[[Pinacol rearrangement|Pinacol]] cascade which produces a [[tetrahydrofuran]], has also been used extensively by the Overman group,<ref name="HirstOverman">{{cite journal|last=Hirst|first=G.C. |author2=T.O. Johnson |author3=L. E. Overman|year=1993|journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society|publisher=ACS|volume=115|pages=2992–2993|doi=10.1021/ja00060a064|title=First total synthesis of Lycopodium alkaloids of the magellanane group. Enantioselective total syntheses of (−)-magellanine and (+)-magellaninone|issue=7 |bibcode=1993JAChS.115.2992H }}</ref> for example in the total synthesis of (–)-[[magellanine]], a ''[[Lycopodium]]'' [[alkaloid]].
